title: Vermeer and the Optical Question
passage:
Since the late nineteenth century, viewers of Johannes Vermeer's paintings have remarked on qualities that seem almost photographic. In works such as View of Delft, small highlights dissolve into diffuse dots of light, and objects in the foreground can appear disproportionately large relative to those behind them. These peculiarities led some art historians to propose that Vermeer composed his pictures with the aid of a camera obscura, a darkened box in which a lens projects an image onto a surface.

The hypothesis is attractive, but the evidence for it is largely circumstantial. No inventory of Vermeer's possessions lists such a device, and no contemporary describes him using one. Moreover, technical analysis of his canvases has found little sign of the tracing one might expect if he had copied projected images directly. Proponents respond that a painter could have consulted the projection to study effects of light without transferring its outlines, a practice that would leave no physical trace.

Skeptics, for their part, concede that Vermeer was probably aware of optical instruments, which were widely discussed in the Dutch Republic, where lens grinding was a flourishing craft. Yet they argue that the so-called optical effects could equally have been achieved through careful observation and deliberate stylization. The diffuse highlights, for instance, may represent a painterly convention rather than an imitation of an out-of-focus lens. The debate thus turns less on what Vermeer saw than on whether his distinctive manner should be attributed to an instrument or to the painter's own judgment.

questions.prompt: The word "circumstantial" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: detailed
indirect
conclusive
incidental
questions.explanation: The evidence is "circumstantial" because it is inferred from features of the paintings rather than shown directly by documents. "Detailed" is a real meaning of the word (a circumstantial account), but the next sentence stresses missing proof, not abundant detail.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, why do proponents believe the lack of tracing does not disprove their hypothesis?
options: Technical analysis has examined too few canvases to detect any tracing.
Projected outlines could be transferred to a canvas without leaving any visible trace.
Vermeer may have looked at the image for guidance without copying its contours.
Inventories of Dutch painters' possessions rarely listed optical devices.
questions.explanation: The last sentence of paragraph 2 says a painter could consult the projection to study light without transferring its outlines. The option about transferring outlines reuses those words but reverses the point, since proponents say the outlines were not transferred.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about the skeptics' position?
options: It holds that the diffuse highlights prove Vermeer never looked through a lens.
It does not depend on showing that Vermeer was unfamiliar with optical instruments.
It rests on documents showing that Vermeer rejected the camera obscura.
It assumes that lens grinding in the Dutch Republic was too primitive to be useful.
questions.explanation: Skeptics concede that Vermeer probably knew of optical instruments, yet argue that his effects could equally come from observation, so their case does not require his ignorance of such devices. The option about highlights is too extreme, since the passage says only that they may be a convention.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention "The diffuse highlights" in paragraph 3?
options: To show that Vermeer deliberately imitated the blurred image of an out-of-focus lens
To identify a painterly convention that Vermeer's contemporaries rejected
To explain why the craft of lens grinding flourished in the Dutch Republic
To give an example of a feature that might be explained without an optical device
questions.explanation: The highlights illustrate the skeptics' claim that apparently optical effects could result from stylization. The option about imitating an out-of-focus lens reuses the passage's words but states the very view the example is meant to challenge.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the essential information in this sentence from paragraph 3? "The debate thus turns less on what Vermeer saw than on whether his distinctive manner should be attributed to an instrument or to the painter's own judgment."
options: The key disagreement concerns the source of his style: a device or his artistic choices.
The debate concerns what Vermeer saw through his instrument rather than how he chose to paint.
Scholars agree about Vermeer's manner but disagree about what he actually saw.
Vermeer's own judgment, not any instrument, produced his distinctive manner.
questions.explanation: The sentence says the dispute is about whether Vermeer's style comes from an instrument or from his judgment. The option claiming his judgment produced the style takes a side, whereas the sentence only describes what the debate is about.

title: Drought and the Maya Collapse
passage:
Between roughly 800 and 950 CE, many of the great cities of the southern Maya lowlands were abandoned. Monument building ceased, royal dynasties vanished from the inscriptions, and populations that had numbered in the millions declined sharply. Explaining this so-called collapse has long been one of the central problems of Mesoamerican archaeology.

Since the 1990s, a climatic explanation has gained considerable support. Sediment cores from lakes in the Yucatán Peninsula record shifts in the ratio of oxygen isotopes and in the deposition of gypsum, a mineral that precipitates when evaporation exceeds rainfall. These records indicate a series of severe droughts during the period of decline. For a society that depended on rain-fed maize and on reservoirs to survive the dry season, repeated droughts may well have been devastating.

Yet many archaeologists caution against regarding drought as a sufficient explanation. The decline was not simultaneous: some cities were abandoned decades before others, and several centers in the drier northern lowlands, notably Chichén Itzá, flourished during the very period when the south was emptying. Inscriptions, moreover, record intensifying warfare among rival kingdoms well before the driest intervals. Many researchers therefore favor a model in which drought acted on a political system already strained by conflict, population pressure, and environmental degradation, so that climate amplified vulnerabilities rather than creating them.

questions.prompt: The word "precipitates" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: acts too hastily
brings on suddenly
separates out as a solid
falls as rain
questions.explanation: Gypsum is a mineral that separates out of lake water as a solid when evaporation is high. "Falls as rain" reflects the weather sense of precipitation, which is the opposite of the dry conditions described in the sentence.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 3, what is one reason that drought alone is considered an insufficient explanation?
options: Lake sediments show that the droughts began only after the decline was underway.
All of the southern cities were abandoned at the same moment.
Inscriptions show that warfare ended before the driest intervals.
Some areas with less rainfall prospered while southern cities declined.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 notes that centers in the drier northern lowlands, such as Chichén Itzá, flourished as the south emptied. The option about warfare reuses the phrase about the driest intervals but reverses it, since warfare intensified before them.

questions.prompt: Based on paragraph 2, what can be inferred about a layer of lake sediment that is unusually rich in gypsum?
options: It probably formed during a relatively dry period.
It probably formed during a period of heavy rainfall.
It probably reveals where maize was once grown.
It probably caused the lake to dry up completely.
questions.explanation: Gypsum forms when evaporation exceeds rainfall, and the cores are used to identify droughts, so a gypsum-rich layer points to dry conditions. The option claiming the gypsum caused the drying reverses cause and effect.

questions.prompt: How does paragraph 3 relate to paragraph 2?
options: It provides further sediment evidence for the droughts in paragraph 2.
It describes how the reservoirs mentioned in paragraph 2 were managed.
It rejects the climate records in paragraph 2 as unreliable and probably misleading.
It qualifies the explanation in paragraph 2 with evidence that it is incomplete.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 accepts that drought mattered but argues it was not sufficient, citing uneven timing and earlier warfare. The option about rejecting the climate records is too extreme, since paragraph 3 never disputes the droughts themselves.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the essential information in this sentence from paragraph 3? "Many researchers therefore favor a model in which drought acted on a political system already strained by conflict, population pressure, and environmental degradation, so that climate amplified vulnerabilities rather than creating them."
options: Researchers favor a model in which drought had little effect on a society that was already declining.
Many scholars think dry conditions worsened existing weaknesses in Maya society rather than producing them.
Researchers believe conflict and population pressure created the droughts that strained the political system.
Most researchers think the climate created vulnerabilities that conflict and degradation later amplified.
questions.explanation: The sentence says drought intensified existing problems rather than causing them. The option in which climate created vulnerabilities later amplified by conflict reverses the roles assigned in the sentence.

title: What Gothic Ribs Really Did
passage:
For much of the nineteenth century, the Gothic cathedral was celebrated as a triumph of engineering logic. The French architect and restorer Eugène Viollet-le-Duc argued that every element of the style had a structural rationale. In his account, the ribs that cross a vault formed a load-bearing skeleton, while the thin stone panels between them were little more than infill, carried by the ribs much as a roof is carried by its rafters.

This rationalist interpretation was challenged in the 1930s by the engineer Pol Abraham, who contended that the ribs were largely ornamental once a vault was complete. His case drew partly on the evidence of churches damaged in the First World War. In several buildings, ribs had been dislodged by shelling, yet the vaults above them remained standing, a result difficult to reconcile with the notion that the ribs bore the weight.

Later studies have tended to adopt a position between these extremes. The ribs, it now appears, may have been valuable during construction, serving as permanent guides that reduced the amount of temporary wooden framework needed to build the vault. They may also have reinforced the vulnerable intersections where curved surfaces meet. Once the mortar had cured, however, the shell is thought to have functioned largely as a unified whole. The ribs, on this view, were neither a mere skeleton nor mere decoration, and their visual prominence may have owed as much to aesthetic preference as to necessity.

questions.prompt: The word "reconcile" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: compare carefully
make consistent
resign oneself to
restore friendship between
questions.explanation: Standing vaults without ribs are hard to make consistent with the idea that ribs carried the load. "Restore friendship between" is a real meaning of "reconcile" when it refers to people, which does not fit a result and a notion.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 3, later studies suggest all of the following about Gothic ribs EXCEPT:
options: They remained the main support of the vault after the mortar had cured.
They may have strengthened the weak points where vault surfaces join.
They helped builders by limiting the timber framework that was required.
Their prominence may partly reflect the taste of the builders.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says that once the mortar cured the shell worked largely as a unified whole, so the ribs were not the main support. The other three options paraphrase claims made in paragraph 3.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 2 about the war-damaged churches?
options: Abraham believed that their vaults had originally been built without any ribs.
Their ribs were dislodged because the mortar between the stones had never properly cured.
The shelling showed that vaults become stronger when their ribs are removed.
Had Viollet-le-Duc been right, the vaults should have fallen once their ribs were lost.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says Viollet-le-Duc saw the ribs as a load-bearing skeleton, and paragraph 2 says vaults stood after losing them, which is why the result was hard to reconcile with his view. The option about vaults becoming stronger goes far beyond the evidence, which shows only that they survived.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention "temporary wooden framework" in paragraph 3?
options: To argue that ribs made temporary supports entirely unnecessary
To show that the ribs were merely ornamental once completed
To explain one way the ribs may have been useful to builders
To identify the material that Gothic builders used for vault panels
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says ribs served as permanent guides that reduced the amount of temporary wooden framework needed. The option claiming supports became entirely unnecessary is too extreme, since the passage says only that less framework was needed.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Viollet-le-Duc's restorations changed how the ribs of Gothic vaults function.
Damage from the First World War proved that Gothic ribs had always been purely decorative.
Gothic vaults were built as unified shells that never needed any ribs at all.
Accounts of the ribs' role have shifted from a purely structural view to a mixed one.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from Viollet-le-Duc's structural view through Abraham's challenge to a later position between the two. The option about wartime damage overstates Abraham's evidence and ignores the compromise view in paragraph 3.

title: The Slow Acceptance of Copernicus
passage:
It is often assumed that Nicolaus Copernicus's heliocentric system, published in 1543, was quickly recognized as superior because it predicted planetary positions more accurately. In fact, its predictive advantage was negligible. Because Copernicus retained the ancient assumption that celestial motions must be perfectly circular, he still required numerous auxiliary circles to fit the observations, and tables computed from his model were not markedly better than those based on Ptolemy.

The case for the new system therefore rested chiefly on other grounds. It explained naturally certain phenomena that the Ptolemaic system could accommodate only by arbitrary adjustments, such as the fact that Mercury and Venus never appear far from the Sun, and it fixed the order and relative distances of the planets. To many astronomers, however, such elegance did not outweigh formidable objections. A moving Earth seemed to contradict both everyday experience and accepted physics, and if the Earth orbited the Sun, the fixed stars ought to show an annual shift in apparent position, which no one could detect.

For several decades, a common response was to use Copernican mathematics as a calculating device while withholding belief in a moving Earth. Tycho Brahe proposed a compromise in which the planets circle the Sun while the Sun circles a stationary Earth. Only in the seventeenth century, after Kepler replaced circles with ellipses and telescopic observations undermined traditional cosmology, did heliocentrism win broad acceptance. The missing stellar shift, it turned out, was real but minute; it was not measured until 1838.

questions.prompt: The word "formidable" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: very numerous
inspiring admiration
hard to overcome
causing terror
questions.explanation: The objections were serious enough to outweigh the system's elegance, so they were hard to overcome. "Inspiring admiration" is a real meaning of "formidable" when praising a person's skill, but objections are not being praised here.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, all of the following counted against the Copernican system EXCEPT:
options: It appeared incompatible with the physics generally accepted at the time.
It could not explain why Mercury and Venus stay close to the Sun.
It predicted a yearly stellar shift that no one could observe.
It conflicted with ordinary experience of a motionless Earth.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 presents the closeness of Mercury and Venus to the Sun as something the Copernican system explained naturally, so it was an advantage. The other three options restate the objections listed later in the paragraph.

questions.prompt: Based on paragraphs 2 and 3, what can be inferred about astronomers in the sixteenth century?
options: They detected a small annual shift but chose to treat it as an error.
They concluded from the missing shift that Tycho's compromise model was the correct one.
They could detect the shift only after Kepler introduced ellipses.
Their instruments were probably not precise enough to reveal the stellar shift.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says no one could detect the shift, and paragraph 3 says it was real but so minute that it was not measured until 1838, implying earlier observations lacked the necessary precision. The option about Tycho goes beyond the passage, which presents his model only as a compromise.

questions.prompt: How does paragraph 3 relate to paragraph 2?
options: It explains why Ptolemy's older system needed the many arbitrary adjustments mentioned in paragraph 2.
It shows that the objections in paragraph 2 were quickly dismissed by most astronomers.
It describes how astronomers dealt with the tension between the merits and objections in paragraph 2.
It offers additional examples of phenomena that the new system explained more naturally.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 weighs elegance against objections, and paragraph 3 describes responses such as using Copernican mathematics without believing in a moving Earth. The option about quick dismissal contradicts the decades of hesitation described in paragraph 3.

questions.prompt: What is the author's attitude toward the assumption described at the beginning of paragraph 1?
options: The author treats it as a misconception about why the system won support.
The author accepts it as broadly accurate for the period after 1543.
The author considers it unimportant to the history of astronomy.
The author finds it plausible but impossible to confirm with surviving evidence.
questions.explanation: The author follows the assumption with "In fact, its predictive advantage was negligible" and explains that support rested on other grounds. The option calling the assumption plausible but unconfirmable ignores that the author directly refutes it.

title: The Meaning of Well-Tempered
passage:
A keyboard instrument cannot be tuned so that every interval is acoustically pure. If fifths are tuned perfectly, a sequence of twelve of them overshoots the starting pitch by a small amount, known as the Pythagorean comma, and this discrepancy must be absorbed somewhere. In the meantone systems common around 1600, it was concentrated in a few rarely used intervals, which made thirds in familiar keys sweet but rendered remote keys virtually unusable.

Johann Sebastian Bach's Well-Tempered Clavier of 1722, which contains a prelude and fugue in each of the twenty-four major and minor keys, was long cited as a manifesto for equal temperament, the system in which the comma is spread evenly so that all keys sound identical in character. Many modern reference works repeated this claim with little qualification.

Historians of tuning now regard that reading as anachronistic. In German usage of the period, "well-tempered" appears to have denoted any arrangement in which all keys were playable, not necessarily one in which they were alike. Several theorists of Bach's time described unequal systems that met this condition while preserving audible differences among keys, so that those with few sharps or flats remained purer than distant ones. Whether Bach favored one of these schemes is uncertain, and attempts to reconstruct his preferred tuning from a decorative pattern on the title page have produced no consensus. What seems clear is that the collection demonstrates the usability of all keys, not their uniformity.

questions.prompt: The word "anachronistic" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: projecting a later idea onto the past
excessively technical
old-fashioned and outdated
inaccurate in many of its smaller details
questions.explanation: Reading "well-tempered" as equal temperament imposes a later idea on an eighteenth-century term. "Old-fashioned" is a real sense of "anachronistic" for customs that outlive their time, but here the error is the reverse: a modern notion applied to an older text.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what was one consequence of meantone tuning?
options: Familiar keys were sacrificed so that remote keys sounded pure.
Twelve perfect fifths fell short of the starting pitch.
Keys far from the familiar ones could hardly be played.
Thirds sounded sweet in every key, including remote ones.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says meantone made thirds sweet in familiar keys but rendered remote keys virtually unusable. The option about sacrificing familiar keys reuses the paragraph's terms but reverses which keys suffered.

questions.prompt: Based on paragraphs 1 and 3, what can be inferred about meantone tuning?
options: It was the system that Bach intended for the Well-Tempered Clavier.
It preserved audible differences while making every key equally usable.
It was regarded by Bach's contemporaries as a form of equal temperament.
It would probably not have counted as "well-tempered" in Bach's time.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says "well-tempered" meant that all keys were playable, while paragraph 1 says meantone left remote keys virtually unusable, so meantone would not qualify. The option about preserving differences describes the unequal systems of paragraph 3, not meantone.

questions.prompt: How does paragraph 3 relate to paragraph 2?
options: It supplies evidence confirming that Bach preferred the system in paragraph 2.
It argues that the reading in paragraph 2 imposes a later meaning on a historical term.
It describes the problem of the comma that paragraph 2 leaves unsolved.
It explains why modern reference works were right to repeat the claim made in paragraph 2.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 presents the traditional equal-temperament reading, and paragraph 3 calls it anachronistic because of what the term meant at the time. The option about confirming Bach's preference reverses the relationship, since paragraph 3 says his preference is uncertain.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the essential information in this sentence from paragraph 3? "Several theorists of Bach's time described unequal systems that met this condition while preserving audible differences among keys, so that those with few sharps or flats remained purer than distant ones."
options: Unequal systems of the time made every key equally pure and so removed all audible differences among the keys.
Because distant keys were impure, theorists of Bach's time described those keys as unplayable.
Theorists of the period preferred keys with many sharps or flats because those keys sounded purer.
Some theorists then proposed tunings in which all keys worked yet still differed, simpler keys sounding purer.
questions.explanation: The sentence says these systems kept all keys playable while letting keys with few sharps or flats remain purer. The option claiming every key was equally pure contradicts the phrase about preserving audible differences.

title: Reconsidering Forager Affluence
passage:
Until the mid-twentieth century, the life of hunter-gatherers was commonly portrayed as a precarious struggle for survival in which the constant search for food left no time for leisure. In 1966 the anthropologist Marshall Sahlins challenged this image in an essay provocatively titled "The Original Affluent Society." Drawing on time-allocation studies of groups such as the Ju/'hoansi of the Kalahari, he argued that foragers obtained adequate food with only a few hours of work a day and that they were affluent not because they possessed much but because they wanted little.

Sahlins's argument was enormously influential, partly because it inverted familiar assumptions about progress. If foraging was so undemanding, then the adoption of agriculture, which typically required longer hours of toil, could no longer be regarded as an obvious improvement, and its spread demanded some other explanation.

Subsequent research has complicated the picture. Critics noted that the early studies counted mainly the time spent acquiring food, omitting the considerable labor of processing it, making tools, and gathering firewood; when these tasks are included, working hours rise substantially. Some observations, moreover, were made during unusually favorable seasons, and the groups studied had long been in contact with herders and farmers, so they may not represent foragers of the distant past. Nonetheless, many anthropologists accept a weaker version of the thesis: that foraging was not necessarily more arduous than early farming, and that the shift to agriculture was not self-evidently beneficial for those who undertook it.

questions.prompt: The word "provocatively" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: in a way meant to stir debate
in a misleading way
in a way meant to attract desire
in a deliberately insulting way
questions.explanation: Calling foragers "affluent" was designed to challenge readers and stir debate about a familiar image. "Deliberately insulting" is a real sense of "provocative" when describing behavior, but the title challenges an idea rather than insulting anyone.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 3, why did critics believe the early studies underestimated foragers' work?
options: The studies measured work only during unfavorable seasons.
The studies largely ignored tasks other than obtaining food.
The studies included time spent trading with nearby farmers.
The studies classified the gathering of firewood as leisure.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the studies counted mainly time spent acquiring food and omitted processing, toolmaking, and gathering firewood. The option about unfavorable seasons reverses the passage, which says some observations came from unusually favorable seasons.

questions.prompt: Based on paragraphs 2 and 3, what can be inferred about the weaker version of Sahlins's thesis?
options: It removes the need to explain why people adopted agriculture.
It shows that farming spread because foraging took longer hours.
It still leaves the spread of agriculture in need of explanation.
It implies that early farmers were wealthier than foragers.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says that if farming was not an obvious improvement, its spread demanded another explanation, and paragraph 3 says the weaker thesis still holds that the shift was not self-evidently beneficial. The option about removing the need for explanation reverses this logic.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention that the groups studied "had long been in contact with herders and farmers" in paragraph 3?
options: To show that they worked longer hours than their herding and farming neighbors
To explain why these particular groups eventually adopted farming
To support Sahlins's claim that foragers wanted relatively little
To question whether they are typical of foragers in the remote past
questions.explanation: The sentence concludes that the groups "may not represent foragers of the distant past," so the contact is cited to raise doubts about how typical they are. The option about adopting farming is unsupported, since the passage never says these groups became farmers.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the essential information in this sentence from paragraph 2? "If foraging was so undemanding, then the adoption of agriculture, which typically required longer hours of toil, could no longer be regarded as an obvious improvement, and its spread demanded some other explanation."
options: Agriculture spread because people came to regard longer hours of toil as an obvious improvement over foraging.
Foraging required longer hours of toil than farming did, so agriculture was clearly an improvement for those who adopted it.
Since farming apparently took more work than foraging, its adoption could not simply be called progress and needed explaining.
Because agriculture was undemanding, its spread required no explanation beyond the fact that it was an improvement.
questions.explanation: The sentence argues that if farming required more work, its adoption cannot be assumed to be an improvement and must be explained in some other way. The option claiming foraging required longer hours reverses the comparison.

title: Revisiting the Rise of the Novel
passage:
In an influential study published in 1957, the critic Ian Watt argued that the English novel emerged in the early eighteenth century as a genuinely new form. Writers such as Daniel Defoe and Samuel Richardson, he contended, broke with earlier fiction by adopting what he called "formal realism": the detailed rendering of ordinary individuals in particular places and times. Watt linked this innovation to the growth of a literate middle class whose tastes and leisure the new form reflected.

Watt's thesis proved remarkably durable, but subsequent scholarship has exposed its limitations. Critics have pointed out that his canon consisted almost entirely of male authors, although women wrote a large proportion of the prose fiction published in the period. Others have argued that the supposed break with the past was less abrupt than Watt implied, since the novel absorbed conventions from romance, spiritual autobiography, and travel narrative, genres he had treated as precursors to be superseded.

Such objections do not necessarily invalidate Watt's insight that something distinctive occurred in these decades. Rather, they suggest that the "rise" he described may have been as much a product of later critical selection as of literary history. The novels he privileged came to define the genre partly because they fit a narrative of progress toward realism, a narrative that obscured the diversity of what eighteenth-century readers actually consumed. Recent histories therefore tend to describe the novel's emergence as gradual and contested rather than as a single decisive origin.

questions.prompt: The word "superseded" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: imitated
replaced
overlooked
preceded
questions.explanation: Watt treated romance and travel narrative as earlier forms that the novel would replace. "Preceded" is tempting because the genres are called precursors, but "superseded" describes what the novel did to them, not their earlier position in time.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, which of the following is NOT a criticism that has been made of Watt's thesis?
options: He paid little attention to fiction written by women.
He made the break with earlier fiction seem sharper than it was.
He treated romance as a form the novel simply left behind.
He exaggerated the size of the literate middle class.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 mentions criticisms of Watt's male canon and of his claim of an abrupt break, including his treatment of earlier genres as precursors. The middle class appears only in paragraph 1 as part of Watt's own argument and is never criticized.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about some eighteenth-century fiction?
options: Widely read works may have been neglected because they did not fit a story of rising realism.
Later critics selected novels chiefly by counting how many copies each had sold.
Eighteenth-century readers mostly preferred the realist novels that Watt later chose to emphasize.
Watt deliberately concealed popular works that contradicted his own argument.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the privileged novels fit a narrative of progress toward realism and that this narrative obscured what readers actually consumed, implying that other widely read works were overlooked. The option about deliberate concealment is too extreme, since the passage attributes the neglect to selection, not intent.

questions.prompt: How does paragraph 3 relate to paragraph 2?
options: It rejects the objections in paragraph 2 as invalid and restores Watt's view.
It offers further examples of the male bias described in paragraph 2.
It restates the evidence for formal realism in greater detail.
It assesses what the objections in paragraph 2 imply for Watt's account.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 begins "Such objections" and explains that they reframe rather than invalidate Watt's insight. The option claiming the objections are rejected misreads "do not necessarily invalidate," which concerns Watt's insight, not the objections.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the author's attitude toward Watt's thesis?
options: It should be abandoned because its canon was entirely male.
It remains durable because it reflects what readers actually consumed.
It captured a real change but needs substantial qualification.
It is of interest only as an example of outdated criticism.
questions.explanation: The author says the objections "do not necessarily invalidate" Watt's insight that something distinctive happened, yet endorses a more gradual, contested account. The option about abandoning the thesis is too extreme and misstates "almost entirely" as "entirely."

title: Monuments Before Farming
passage:
Archaeologists long assumed that monumental architecture appeared only after the development of farming. Agriculture, the reasoning went, generated the food surpluses and settled populations needed to support large construction projects, and organized religion, with its temples and specialists, followed in turn.

The excavation of Göbekli Tepe in southeastern Turkey, begun in the 1990s, appeared to overturn this sequence. The site contains massive circular enclosures built of T-shaped limestone pillars, some over five meters tall and carved with images of foxes, snakes, and vultures. Dating from about 9500 BCE, they were erected by people who had not yet domesticated plants or animals. The principal excavator, Klaus Schmidt, interpreted the site as a ritual center visited by dispersed groups of hunter-gatherers, and he even suggested that the need to feed workers assembled for construction might itself have encouraged the cultivation of wild cereals.

More recent fieldwork has tempered this interpretation. Excavators have identified features such as rock-cut cisterns for collecting water and large quantities of tools for grinding plant foods, which suggest that people may have lived at the site rather than merely gathering there periodically. If so, Göbekli Tepe may represent a settled community whose buildings served social as well as ritual functions. This revision does not restore the old sequence, since the builders were still foragers, but it does weaken the image of a sanctuary set apart from daily life. The site thus indicates that complex social organization could precede farming, though the precise relationship remains uncertain.

questions.prompt: The word "tempered" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: postponed
angered
hardened
moderated
questions.explanation: Recent fieldwork moderated Schmidt's interpretation by suggesting the site was also lived in. "Hardened" is a real meaning of "tempered" for metal, but the new evidence softened the interpretation rather than strengthening it.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, all of the following are true of Göbekli Tepe EXCEPT:
options: Its excavator saw it as a meeting place for scattered groups.
It was built before plants had been domesticated.
Its builders kept domesticated animals beside the enclosures.
Its pillars bear carved images of several wild animals.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the builders had not yet domesticated plants or animals. The carvings, the early date, and Schmidt's view of a center visited by dispersed groups are all stated in paragraph 2.

questions.prompt: Based on paragraphs 1 and 2, what can be inferred about Schmidt's view?
options: It held that religious specialists at the site were the first people to invent agriculture.
It agreed that food surpluses had to exist before construction could begin.
It assumed that the builders had already domesticated wild cereals.
It treated ceremonial building as a possible cause of farming, not a result of it.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the old view saw farming as the basis for monuments, while paragraph 2 reports Schmidt's suggestion that feeding construction workers may have encouraged cultivation, reversing the order. The option about food surpluses restates the older view he challenged.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention "rock-cut cisterns for collecting water and large quantities of tools for grinding plant foods" in paragraph 3?
options: To present evidence that people may have resided at the site
To show that the site was used only for occasional ritual feasts
To prove that the builders were farmers rather than foragers
To explain how the limestone pillars were cut and decorated
questions.explanation: The paragraph says these features suggest people may have lived at the site rather than visiting periodically. The option about farmers contradicts the statement that the builders were still foragers.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Göbekli Tepe was an agricultural village whose carved pillars served no ritual purpose at all.
A site once seen as a foragers' sanctuary still upsets old assumptions, though its role is now seen differently.
New evidence from Göbekli Tepe has restored the traditional view that farming came before any monumental building.
Göbekli Tepe proves that agriculture was invented specifically to feed the builders of temples.
questions.explanation: The passage shows the site upsetting the farming-first sequence and then describes a revised view of it as a settled community. The option about restoring the old view contradicts paragraph 3, which says the revision does not restore the old sequence.

title: The Regularity of Sound Change
passage:
In the early nineteenth century, scholars comparing the Germanic languages with Latin, Greek, and Sanskrit noticed systematic correspondences among their consonants. Where Latin has p, as in pater, English and its relatives typically have f, as in father; where Latin has t, Germanic often has a sound like th. Jacob Grimm codified these patterns in 1822, and Grimm's Law offered compelling evidence that the languages descended from a common ancestor.

The correspondences were not perfect, however. Old English fæder, "father," has a d where the law predicts a th-like sound, while brōþor, "brother," shows the expected sound. For decades such exceptions were tolerated as irregularities. In 1875 the Danish linguist Karl Verner demonstrated that many of them were themselves regular: the outcome depended on the position of the accent in the ancestral word, which can be reconstructed from Sanskrit and Greek.

Verner's discovery had consequences beyond the sounds involved. It emboldened a group of younger scholars, the Neogrammarians, to assert that sound changes operate without exceptions: apparent counterexamples must reflect either an undiscovered conditioning factor, as in Verner's case, or the interference of other processes, such as borrowing or analogy with related forms. The principle was enormously productive, since it compelled researchers to explain every irregularity rather than dismiss it. Later linguists have questioned whether sound change is truly exceptionless, noting that some changes appear to spread gradually through the vocabulary. Even so, the assumption of regularity remains the methodological foundation of historical linguistics.

questions.prompt: The word "codified" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: made into binding law
converted into a secret code
organized into a system
discovered by accident
questions.explanation: Grimm set out the sound correspondences systematically. "Made into binding law" reflects the legal use of "codify," but the patterns were descriptive regularities, not rules anyone enacted.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, what did Verner show about many exceptions to Grimm's Law?
options: They had to be tolerated as irregular because the ancestral accent could not be recovered.
They obeyed a rule of their own, tied to where the stress fell in the older word.
They showed that Grimm had reconstructed the wrong ancestral language.
They resulted from words borrowed into Germanic from Sanskrit and Greek.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says Verner showed the outcome depended on the position of the accent in the ancestral word. The option about borrowing from Sanskrit and Greek reuses those names, but the passage says those languages were used to reconstruct the accent.

questions.prompt: Based on paragraph 3, how would a Neogrammarian most likely respond to a word that seemed to violate a well-established sound law?
options: By assuming that the change spread gradually through the vocabulary
By accepting the word as one of the law's natural irregularities
By concluding that the sound law should be abandoned
By looking for a cause other than a genuine exception to the law
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says Neogrammarians held that sound laws have no exceptions and that counterexamples reflect hidden conditions, borrowing, or analogy. The option about gradual spread describes the view of later critics, not of the Neogrammarians.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention "Old English fæder" in paragraph 2?
options: To illustrate the kind of irregularity that Verner later explained
To suggest that the word was borrowed from a neighboring Germanic language
To give an example of the regular pattern that Grimm codified
To show that Grimm's Law applies to English but not to Latin
questions.explanation: Fæder has a d where Grimm's Law predicts a th-like sound, and the paragraph goes on to say Verner showed such exceptions were regular. The option about the regular pattern describes brōþor, which shows the expected sound.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the essential information in this sentence from paragraph 3? "The principle was enormously productive, since it compelled researchers to explain every irregularity rather than dismiss it."
options: Researchers dismissed the principle because it produced too many irregularities to explain.
Because irregularities were so numerous, researchers were compelled to dismiss most of them.
Insisting on regularity proved fruitful because it forced scholars to account for each anomaly.
The principle was productive, although researchers could explain only a few irregularities.
questions.explanation: The sentence credits the principle's success to the way it required an explanation for every irregularity. The option about compelled dismissal reuses the words compelled and dismiss but reverses the relationship.

title: Movable Type in East and West
passage:
Movable type was not a European invention. In China, the artisan Bi Sheng produced type from baked clay in the eleventh century, and in Korea metal type was used to print a Buddhist text, the Jikji, in 1377, decades before Johannes Gutenberg's press. Yet in East Asia movable type never displaced woodblock printing, whereas in Europe it rapidly became the dominant technology. Historians have offered several explanations for this divergence.

The most frequently cited is linguistic. A printer of Chinese required many thousands of distinct characters, so that casting, storing, and retrieving type demanded enormous investment and labor. European alphabets, by contrast, needed only a few dozen letters plus punctuation. Woodblock printing, moreover, offered real advantages to East Asian printers: carved blocks could be stored and reprinted on demand, allowing small print runs, and they reproduced calligraphy and illustrations with ease.

Some historians caution that the linguistic argument, though valid, is incomplete. The economics of the book trade also differed. In Europe, printing developed as a commercial enterprise in competitive urban markets, where large editions could be sold quickly to recover the high initial costs of a press and type. Much early East Asian movable-type printing, by contrast, was sponsored by states or monasteries for limited distribution, which reduced the pressure to adopt the most efficient method of mass production. The script, in this view, made movable type costly, but institutional circumstances determined whether that cost was worth bearing.

questions.prompt: The word "divergence" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: difference in outcome
loss of attention
open disagreement
departure from a rule
questions.explanation: The divergence is the different fate of movable type in East Asia and Europe. "Open disagreement" is a real meaning, as in a divergence of opinion, but the sentence compares the outcomes in two regions, not the views of historians.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, what was one advantage of woodblocks for East Asian printers?
options: A complete set of blocks needed only a few dozen characters.
Additional copies could be produced whenever they were needed.
Blocks allowed very large editions to be sold quickly.
Blocks were cheaper to cast and store than metal type.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says carved blocks could be stored and reprinted on demand, allowing small print runs. The option about large editions describes European commercial printing in paragraph 3, not woodblocks.

questions.prompt: Based on paragraph 3, what can be inferred about printing for limited distribution?
options: It made the large initial expense of movable type harder to justify.
It was cheaper with movable type than with carved woodblocks.
It encouraged state sponsors to favor methods suited to mass production.
It was more common in European cities than in East Asian monasteries.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says European printers recovered high initial costs by selling large editions, while East Asian sponsors printed for limited distribution, so the cost was harder to recover. The option about favoring mass production reverses the statement that limited distribution reduced that pressure.

questions.prompt: How does paragraph 3 relate to paragraph 2?
options: It gives further evidence about the large number of Chinese characters required.
It explains why woodblocks reproduced calligraphy so easily.
It rejects the linguistic account in paragraph 2 as invalid.
It adds an economic factor to the linguistic account in paragraph 2.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 calls the linguistic argument "valid" but "incomplete" and adds differences in the book trade. The option claiming paragraph 3 rejects the linguistic account ignores that concession.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the essential information in this sentence from paragraph 3? "The script, in this view, made movable type costly, but institutional circumstances determined whether that cost was worth bearing."
options: The script alone determined both the cost of movable type and whether it was adopted.
Because movable type was costly, institutions everywhere refused to bear its expense.
The script raised the expense, yet the setting of printing decided whether paying it made sense.
Institutions made movable type costly, so the script alone determined whether it would be adopted.
questions.explanation: The sentence divides the roles: the script created the cost, and institutions decided whether the cost was worthwhile. The option assigning the cost to institutions and the decision to the script swaps those roles.

title: Molyneux's Problem
passage:
In 1688 the Irish scientist William Molyneux posed a question to John Locke that would occupy philosophers for centuries. Suppose a man born blind has learned to distinguish a cube from a sphere by touch. If his sight were suddenly restored, could he tell which was which merely by looking? Molyneux and Locke both answered no, reasoning that the connection between how a shape feels and how it looks must be learned.

The question was not merely academic, since it bore on a fundamental dispute about the origins of knowledge. Empiricists held that ideas derive from sensory experience, and a negative answer suited their position, as it implied that the senses deliver distinct kinds of information that become linked only through association. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, by contrast, argued that the newly sighted man could in principle reason his way to the answer, since geometry is common to both senses.

Once surgeons began removing cataracts in the eighteenth century, it seemed that experiment might settle the matter. A celebrated report of 1728 described a boy who, after his operation, could not identify by sight objects he knew by touch. Yet such cases proved less decisive than hoped. Patients whose eyes had long been clouded rarely saw clearly immediately after surgery, so their failures might reflect poor vision rather than an inability to connect the senses. Some modern studies have found that patients fail at first but succeed within days, a result each side has read as favoring its own view.

questions.prompt: The word "academic" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: of purely theoretical interest
difficult to understand
learned and scholarly
connected with a university or college
questions.explanation: Saying the question was "not merely academic" means it was not of purely theoretical interest but bore on a fundamental dispute. "Connected with a university" is a real meaning of the word in other contexts but makes no sense here.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 3, all of the following are true of the cataract cases EXCEPT:
options: Some patients in later studies succeeded after a short delay.
One early patient failed to recognize familiar objects by sight.
Patients often could not see well just after the operation.
They led most philosophers to adopt Leibniz's answer.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the cases were less decisive than they appeared and that each side reads the modern results in its own favor, so they did not win most philosophers over to Leibniz. The other options restate details from the paragraph.

questions.prompt: Based on paragraphs 2 and 3, why could empiricists regard the modern findings as support for their view?
options: The patients' long-clouded vision showed that geometry is common to both sight and touch.
The patients' early failure suggests that the link between the senses must be acquired.
The patients succeeded without ever needing to touch the objects again.
The patients in modern studies had been able to see before their illness.
questions.explanation: Empiricists held that the senses are linked only through association, and the patients failed at first before succeeding, which fits a link that must be learned. The option about succeeding without touching would better suit Leibniz's side, not the empiricists'.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention that patients "rarely saw clearly immediately after surgery" in paragraph 3?
options: To show that cataract operations rarely succeeded in the eighteenth century
To suggest that the report of 1728 was invented by the surgeon
To explain why early surgical evidence failed to settle the question
To support Locke's view that the senses are linked through experience
questions.explanation: The detail shows that patients' failures might reflect poor vision rather than an inability to connect the senses, which is why the cases were less decisive than they seemed. The option about Locke's view is wrong because the detail weakens, rather than supports, any conclusion from the failures.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Leibniz showed that a man born blind could reason about geometry by touch alone.
A thought experiment about sight and touch raised deep questions that apparent tests have not resolved.
Cataract surgery eventually proved beyond doubt that Molyneux and Locke had answered the question correctly.
Empiricists and their critics agreed that experiments could never address Molyneux's question.
questions.explanation: The passage presents the question, explains its philosophical stakes, and shows that surgical evidence remains open to rival interpretations. The option about cataract surgery proving Locke right contradicts the statement that such cases were less decisive than they appeared.

title: Silver and the Price Revolution
passage:
Over the sixteenth century, prices in western Europe rose several-fold after a long period of relative stability. Contemporaries were bewildered by the phenomenon, and in 1568 the French political theorist Jean Bodin offered an explanation that has remained influential: the principal cause, he argued, was the abundance of gold and silver, much of it flowing from Spain's American colonies.

Bodin's reasoning anticipated what economists later formalized as the quantity theory of money, which holds that, other things being equal, an increase in the stock of money raises the general level of prices. The timing appears to support it. Imports of American silver increased dramatically after the opening of the rich mines at Potosí in the 1540s, and prices continued to climb as the bullion spread through European trade.

Economic historians have since identified difficulties with this monetary account. In several regions, prices had begun to rise before American silver arrived in significant quantities, and the increase was steepest for grain, whereas manufactured goods became only modestly more expensive. Such a pattern is more consistent with population growth, which resumed after the late medieval epidemics and pressed on a limited supply of land and food. Most historians now regard the two explanations as complementary rather than rival: rising population may have initiated the inflation, while expanding money supplies, including increased output from central European silver mines, allowed it to persist.

questions.prompt: The word "anticipated" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: foreshadowed
looked forward to
expected
prevented
questions.explanation: Bodin's reasoning foreshadowed a theory that economists formalized later. "Expected" is the most common meaning of "anticipate," but Bodin was not expecting the theory; his argument resembled it before it existed.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT mentioned in the passage as evidence bearing on the causes of the price rise?
options: Silver imports grew sharply after new mines opened.
Wages rose faster than the price of grain.
Prices rose in some places before much silver arrived.
Grain became far more expensive than manufactured goods.
questions.explanation: The passage never discusses wages. The early rise in prices and the contrast between grain and manufactured goods appear in paragraph 3, and the growth of silver imports appears in paragraph 2.

questions.prompt: Based on paragraph 3, what can be inferred about a price rise caused mainly by more money?
options: It would cause population to grow by increasing the supply of food.
It would raise the price of grain much faster than that of other goods.
It would be expected to affect the prices of different goods more evenly.
It would begin before silver had arrived in significant quantities.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says the uneven pattern, with grain rising most, fits population growth better, which implies that a purely monetary cause would affect prices more uniformly. The option about grain rising fastest describes the observed pattern that the passage attributes to population pressure.

questions.prompt: How does paragraph 3 relate to paragraph 2?
options: It confirms the argument from timing in paragraph 2 with new evidence from the price of grain.
It explains how economists formalized the theory described in paragraph 2.
It replaces the monetary account in paragraph 2 entirely with a demographic one.
It casts doubt on the support offered in paragraph 2 and reaches a combined explanation.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 challenges the timing evidence of paragraph 2 but concludes that the two explanations are "complementary rather than rival." The option about replacing the monetary account entirely is too extreme, since money supply is still said to have allowed inflation to persist.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the author's view of Bodin's explanation?
options: It is irrelevant to modern discussions of the price rise.
It identified a real cause but cannot explain the inflation on its own.
It is fully confirmed by the timing of the silver imports from Potosí.
It has been entirely refuted by later economic historians of the period.
questions.explanation: The author presents difficulties with the monetary account but ends by treating money supply as one of two complementary causes. The option claiming full refutation ignores the role the author still gives to expanding money supplies.

title: The Painted Statues of Greece
passage:
For eighteenth-century art theorists, the gleaming white marble of ancient Greek statues embodied an ideal of noble simplicity. Johann Joachim Winckelmann, whose writings shaped Neoclassical taste, maintained that the whiter a statue was, the more beautiful it was, and generations of sculptors emulated what they took to be the colorless purity of antiquity.

That ideal rested on a misapprehension. Excavations in the nineteenth century uncovered sculptures and architectural fragments bearing unmistakable traces of paint, and ancient authors occasionally refer to the painting of statues as a skilled craft. Some scholars nonetheless resisted the evidence, suggesting that the colors were later additions or that they had been confined to small details such as eyes and the borders of garments. Since pigments fade and flake when exposed to air and soil, the surviving traces are faint, which made such reservations easier to sustain.

Recent techniques have largely overcome this difficulty. Ultraviolet light and raking illumination can reveal patterns invisible to the naked eye, while chemical analysis can identify specific pigments, including costly minerals such as cinnabar and the synthetic pigment Egyptian blue. Reconstructions based on these findings show figures with richly patterned garments and tinted skin. Their accuracy remains a matter of debate; critics note that the reconstructions often apply flat, saturated colors, whereas ancient painters may have used subtle gradations that left little trace. What is no longer seriously disputed is that the monochrome antiquity admired by Winckelmann was largely an artifact of time and decay.

questions.prompt: The word "misapprehension" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: mistaken belief
anxious expectation
partial understanding
legal arrest
questions.explanation: The white-marble ideal rested on a mistaken belief about how ancient statues looked. "Anxious expectation" is a real meaning of the related word "apprehension," but it does not describe the basis of an aesthetic ideal.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, why was it easier for some scholars to doubt the evidence of paint?
options: Color had been found only on the eyes and the borders of garments.
Ancient authors almost never mentioned the painting of statues.
Little visible color survived because pigments deteriorate over time.
Paint had been added to many sculptures after their excavation.
questions.explanation: The last sentence of paragraph 2 says pigments fade and flake, leaving faint traces that made doubts easier to sustain. The option about eyes and garment borders repeats what the doubters suggested, not the reason their doubts were easier to hold.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraphs 1 and 3 about Neoclassical sculptors?
options: They applied costly pigments such as cinnabar to the surfaces of white marble.
They imitated a look of ancient art that was largely the product of decay.
They deliberately ignored the painted statues that excavators had already uncovered.
They painted their statues in the subtle gradations used by ancient artists.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says these sculptors imitated the colorless purity of antiquity, and paragraph 3 says that monochrome look was largely produced by time and decay. The option about ignoring excavated statues is unsupported, since the passage dates those excavations to the nineteenth century.

questions.prompt: How does paragraph 3 relate to paragraph 2?
options: It describes methods that address the evidential problem raised at the end of paragraph 2.
It shows that the traces of paint described in paragraph 2 were in fact later additions by restorers.
It returns to the Neoclassical ideal introduced at the start of paragraph 2.
It supports the scholars in paragraph 2 who confined color to small details.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 ends by noting that faint traces made doubts easier to sustain, and paragraph 3 opens by saying new techniques have "largely overcome this difficulty." The option about the Neoclassical ideal refers to a different paragraph, since that ideal is introduced in paragraph 1.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the essential information in this sentence from paragraph 3? "Their accuracy remains a matter of debate; critics note that the reconstructions often apply flat, saturated colors, whereas ancient painters may have used subtle gradations that left little trace."
options: Because subtle gradations left little trace, the bold reconstructions are now generally accepted as fully accurate.
The reconstructions are debated because ancient painters avoided applying color to skin and garments.
Critics agree that ancient painters used flat, saturated colors that left little trace on the statues.
Critics doubt the reconstructions, since their bold, uniform colors may miss the subtler shading of ancient painters.
questions.explanation: The sentence questions the reconstructions because their flat, strong colors may not reflect subtler ancient techniques. The option claiming ancient painters used flat colors reverses the contrast drawn with the word whereas.

title: Plague and the Fate of Serfdom
passage:
The Black Death of 1347 to 1351 killed perhaps a third or more of Europe's population. In western Europe, the resulting shortage of labor appears to have shifted bargaining power toward surviving peasants and workers. Wages rose despite legislation, such as England's Statute of Labourers of 1351, that attempted to hold them at pre-plague levels, and over the following century many of the labor obligations of serfdom gradually lapsed.

A straightforward demographic explanation would predict similar outcomes wherever labor became scarce. Yet in much of central and eastern Europe, including Poland and Prussia, the centuries after the plague saw the opposite development: lords imposed heavier labor services and tighter restrictions on peasant movement, a process historians call the "second serfdom." Population loss alone, then, cannot account for these divergent trajectories.

Historians have advanced several explanations. Some emphasize the relative strength of competing groups: where towns were numerous and royal authority could check the nobility, peasants had alternatives and allies, whereas in the east a powerful landed nobility faced few such constraints. Others point to commercial incentives, noting that growing demand for grain in western European cities made it profitable for eastern landowners to produce for export using coerced labor. These accounts are not incompatible, and the evidence suggests that a scarcity of labor tended to benefit workers only where political and economic structures allowed them to exploit it.

questions.prompt: The word "lapsed" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: fell out of use
declined in quality
slipped briefly
were overturned
questions.explanation: The obligations of serfdom gradually fell out of use over a century. "Were overturned" suggests sudden, deliberate reversal, which conflicts with the word "gradually" in the same sentence.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what was the aim of England's Statute of Labourers?
options: To abolish the labor obligations that serfs owed their lords
To raise the wages of peasants and workers who had survived
To keep pay from climbing above its level before the epidemic
To record how many workers had died during the epidemic
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the statute attempted to hold wages at pre-plague levels. The option about raising wages describes what actually happened despite the statute, not what it was meant to do.

questions.prompt: Based on paragraphs 2 and 3, what can be inferred about the relationship between western and eastern Europe?
options: Western cities imported grain because their own serfs refused to work.
Economic growth in the west may have helped strengthen serfdom in the east.
Eastern landowners exported grain because the plague had spared their lands.
Grain exports allowed eastern peasants to bargain for higher wages.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 describes heavier labor services in the east, and paragraph 3 says western demand for grain made coerced labor profitable for eastern landowners. The option about eastern peasants bargaining reverses the outcome, since their conditions worsened.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention "Poland and Prussia" in paragraph 2?
options: To give examples of places where the obligations of serfdom gradually lapsed after the plague
To identify the regions where the Black Death caused the greatest losses
To illustrate areas with numerous towns and strong royal authority
To name regions where events defied what a labor shortage alone would predict
questions.explanation: Poland and Prussia are examples of the second serfdom, the opposite of what a simple demographic explanation predicts. The option about serfdom lapsing describes western Europe in paragraph 1.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best expresses the essential information in this sentence from paragraph 3? "These accounts are not incompatible, and the evidence suggests that a scarcity of labor tended to benefit workers only where political and economic structures allowed them to exploit it."
options: The explanations can coexist, and scarce labor mainly helped workers where institutions let them use it.
The explanations agree that labor scarcity benefited workers everywhere, whatever the political structures.
The accounts show that workers exploited political structures in order to create a scarcity of labor.
The accounts conflict, but political structures allowed lords to exploit workers wherever labor was scarce.
questions.explanation: The sentence says the explanations can both be true and that labor shortage helped workers only under favorable structures. The option saying the accounts conflict contradicts the phrase not incompatible and misassigns who did the exploiting.

title: Notation as a Memory Aid
passage:
The earliest surviving notation for Western liturgical chant, dating from the ninth and tenth centuries, consists of neumes, small marks written above the words. Neumes indicate whether the melody rises or falls and how notes are grouped, but in most early sources they do not specify exact pitches or intervals. To modern eyes such notation can seem frustratingly imprecise, and it was once regarded as a mere stage on the way to a more complete system.

Many scholars now interpret the evidence differently. Chant had been transmitted orally for generations before it was written down, and singers learned an extensive repertory by heart. A notation that presupposed this knowledge did not need to record every pitch; it needed only to prompt the memory and to convey nuances of delivery that memory alone might not preserve. Indeed, some early manuscripts include detailed signs for lengthening or lightening notes, information that later, more "precise" notations often omitted.

A different kind of notation became necessary as the repertory grew and church authorities sought uniform practice across regions. In the early eleventh century, the monk Guido of Arezzo promoted a system of lines spaced a third apart, on which neumes could be placed to fix their relative pitch. Guido claimed that his method let singers learn in days melodies that had once taken years. The innovation laid the foundation for modern staff notation, yet it may also have hastened the decline of the oral skills that earlier notation had been designed to support.

questions.prompt: The word "presupposed" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: imposed
took for granted
concealed
predicted in advance
questions.explanation: The notation took for granted that singers already knew the melodies, so it did not need to record every pitch. "Predicted in advance" is tempting because of the prefix pre-, but the notation was assuming existing knowledge, not predicting future events.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, early neumes recorded all of the following EXCEPT:
options: the exact interval between one note and the next
the way in which notes were grouped together
the direction in which the melody moved
details such as whether a note was lengthened
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says early neumes did not specify exact pitches or intervals. Direction and grouping are named in paragraph 1, and signs for lengthening notes are mentioned in paragraph 2.

questions.prompt: Based on paragraphs 2 and 3, what can be inferred about the adoption of staff notation?
options: It was opposed by church authorities who wanted practice to remain regional.
It made it impossible for singers to memorize any part of the chant repertory.
It involved a trade-off, gaining exact pitch while possibly losing details of performance.
It restored the nuances of delivery that the earlier oral tradition had allowed to disappear.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says later, more "precise" notations often omitted signs for delivery, and paragraph 3 says lines fixed relative pitch, so precision came at some cost. The option about restoring nuances reverses the passage, which links their loss to later notation.

questions.prompt: How does paragraph 3 relate to paragraph 2?
options: It describes how oral transmission eventually replaced the notation in paragraph 2.
It presents new evidence that undermines the interpretation of early neumes offered in paragraph 2.
It gives further examples of the signs for lengthening notes mentioned in paragraph 2.
It explains how changing circumstances made the notation described in paragraph 2 insufficient.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains why memory-based neumes were adequate, and paragraph 3 explains that a growing repertory and the push for uniformity created a need for something different. Paragraph 3 does not undermine paragraph 2; it builds on its account of what the older notation was for.

questions.prompt: The author's attitude toward Guido's innovation can best be described as
options: wholly enthusiastic about its role in modern notation
appreciative of its benefits but alert to a possible cost
indifferent, since it merely continued earlier monastic practice
dismissive, since it was less precise than the neumes
questions.explanation: The author credits the system with founding modern staff notation but adds that it "may also have hastened the decline" of oral skills. The option calling the author wholly enthusiastic ignores that final reservation.

title: The Spread of the Bantu Languages
passage:
Today some five hundred Bantu languages are spoken across much of sub-Saharan Africa, from Cameroon to South Africa. Comparative linguistics indicates that their common ancestor was spoken in a relatively small area near the present border of Nigeria and Cameroon, roughly four to five thousand years ago. The extraordinary spread of this family is one of the most consequential episodes in African history, yet its mechanisms are still debated.

The prevailing interpretation holds that the languages were carried by migrating farming communities. Archaeological evidence for the spread of pottery, of cereal and yam cultivation, and later of ironworking roughly parallels the pattern reconstructed by linguists, and genetic studies of modern populations indicate substantial movement of people from west-central Africa toward the east and south. On this view, farmers with growing populations gradually expanded into regions occupied by foragers, many of whom were absorbed or displaced.

Yet the correspondence among languages, artifacts, and genes is imperfect. Ironworking, for instance, appears in some regions before Bantu languages are thought to have arrived and in others considerably later, suggesting that technologies sometimes circulated independently of speakers. Linguists also debate whether the expansion followed a single route through the equatorial rainforest or divided early into eastern and western streams. Some scholars stress that language shift, in which local groups adopted the speech of newcomers for social or economic reasons, may have contributed alongside migration. The emerging picture is thus one of a broadly demographic process whose details varied considerably from region to region.

questions.prompt: The word "consequential" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: frequently repeated
following logically
important in its effects
self-important
questions.explanation: The spread of the Bantu languages is described as having far-reaching effects on African history. "Following logically" is a real meaning related to "consequent," but the sentence is about significance, not logical sequence.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, all of the following support the view that farming communities carried the languages EXCEPT:
options: the match between archaeological and linguistic patterns
the spread of pottery and of cereal and yam cultivation
genetic evidence of people moving toward the east and south
the separate movement of ironworking among foraging peoples
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 cites pottery, crops, genetic evidence, and the parallel with linguistic patterns. The independent circulation of technology appears in paragraph 3 as a complication for that view, not as support.

questions.prompt: Based on paragraphs 2 and 3, what can be inferred about ironworking as evidence?
options: Its presence cannot by itself reliably mark the arrival of Bantu speakers.
It shows that Bantu speakers learned metalworking from the foragers they met.
It spread along a single route through the equatorial rainforest.
It is absent from every region where Bantu languages are spoken today.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 lists ironworking among the traces that parallel the languages, but paragraph 3 says it appears earlier in some regions and later in others, so it is an unreliable marker. The option about a single route confuses ironworking with the linguists' debate about the expansion's path.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention "language shift" in paragraph 3?
options: To explain why ironworking reached some regions much later than the languages did
To show how linguists located the region where the family began
To present a process other than migration that may have spread the languages
To argue that no significant movement of people took place
questions.explanation: Language shift is offered as something that "may have contributed alongside migration." The option claiming no movement of people took place is too extreme, since the passage still calls the process broadly demographic.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Ironworking was the technology that allowed Bantu-speaking farmers to displace foragers throughout Africa.
The Bantu languages' spread is largely credited to farming migrants, though evidence points to a regionally varied process.
Linguistic evidence about the Bantu languages has been shown to contradict the genetic and archaeological record.
The Bantu languages spread solely because foragers across the continent chose to adopt the speech of their farming neighbors.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 presents the migration view, and paragraph 3 qualifies it, concluding that the process varied by region. The option about ironworking is wrong because paragraph 3 says ironworking sometimes moved independently of speakers.

title: The Great Vowel Shift
passage:
Between roughly 1400 and 1700, the long vowels of English underwent a series of changes known as the Great Vowel Shift. Each long vowel was raised, that is, pronounced with the tongue higher in the mouth, and the two highest vowels, which could rise no further, became diphthongs. Thus a word such as bite, once pronounced with a vowel resembling that of modern "beet," acquired its present sound, while the vowel of beet had earlier resembled that of modern "bait."

Because English spelling had begun to stabilize before the shift was complete, partly through the influence of printing after the 1470s, many words retain spellings that reflect their medieval pronunciation. This mismatch accounts for much of the irregularity that learners find so vexing.

Why the shift occurred is far less certain. One explanation holds that it unfolded as a chain reaction: as one vowel moved, it encroached on the space of its neighbor, which shifted in turn to keep words distinct. Linguists disagree, however, about whether the high vowels moved first, creating gaps that lower vowels were drawn into, or whether lower vowels moved first, pushing the higher ones upward. Other scholars doubt that the changes formed a single coherent event at all, observing that they were spread over three centuries and did not proceed identically in all dialects. Some have also proposed a social dimension: migration to London after the plague brought speakers of different dialects into contact, and certain pronunciations may have spread as markers of prestige.

questions.prompt: The word "encroached" in the passage is closest in meaning to
options: drew near
relied
intruded
spread out
